Push the project to GitHub with a .gitignore that excludes .env , __pycache__/ , and .venv/ . 7.
Mini Project
'Environment Health Check CLI' - Build a small command-line script, healthcheck.py , that:
Loads all required environment variables and reports which are missing. ·
Pings OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google AI Studio with a trivial request each, reporting latency and success/failure for each. ·
Confirms Docker is running by checking docker info via subprocess . ·
Outputs a clean, color-coded summary (use the rich library) of environment readiness. ·
This becomes a genuinely useful tool you'll reuse (and extend) throughout the rest of the handbook.
Assignment
Extend the Health Check CLI to also verify PostgreSQL and Redis connectivity (even though we haven't used them yet - install them now via Docker Compose so Module 8 and Module 16 have zero setup friction). Write a docker-compose.yml that spins up both, and have the CLI attempt a connection to each.
Coding Exercises
Write a function load_required_env(names: list[str]) -> dict that raises a clear, custom exception listing all missing variables at once (not just the first one). 1.
Write a function that redacts an API key for safe logging (e.g., sk-ab...wxyz instead of the full key). 2.
Write a .gitignore generator function that takes a project type ('python', 'node') and writes an appropriate .gitignore . 3.
Write a retry decorator ( @retry(max_attempts=3, backoff=2) ) usable on any API call function. 4.
Write a function that measures and returns the latency of an arbitrary callable. 5.
Write a function that validates an OpenAI-style API key's format (starts with sk-, correct length range) before even attempting a network call. 6.
Write a small config validator using pydantic.BaseSettings (or pydantic-settings ) instead of manual os.environ calls, and explain the trade-off vs. the manual approach.

Security is catching up to a new threat surface. Prompt injection, data exfiltration through tool calls, and unsafe autonomous actions are real production risks, not academic curiosities. AI Security (Module 25) is no longer optional reading. 5.
AI Engineer vs. ML Engineer vs. LLM Engineer vs. Prompt Engineer vs. AI Solutions Architect vs. Agentic AI Engineer
These titles get used loosely in job postings, which causes real confusion. Here's a grounded comparison based on what each role actually does day to day.
A useful mental model: ML Engineers build the model. LLM Engineers work close to the model internals. Prompt Engineers get the most out of an existing model through instructions alone. AI/GenAI Engineers build products around models. Agentic AI Engineers build products where the model takes autonomous multi-step action. AI Solutions Architects decide how all of the above fit together at an organizational level.
This handbook is built specifically to take you to AI Engineer , with a strong on-ramp into Agentic AI Engineer - the two roles with the fastest-growing hiring demand in 2026, and the roles most directly reachable from a Data Science background.
Who Should Use This Handbook
Data Scientists who know Python, pandas, and modeling but have never shipped a production API or built an LLM-powered application. ·
Junior/Backend Developers who are comfortable with software engineering but new to LLMs, embeddings, and agents. ·
Freshers and career switchers with basic Python literacy who are targeting AI Engineer roles directly. ·
Engineering teams onboarding new hires into an AI platform team, using this as a structured internal curriculum. ·
Prerequisites
Before starting, you should already be comfortable with:
Python fundamentals - variables, functions, classes, loops, list/dict comprehensions, virtual environments, pip. ·
Basic command line usage - navigating directories, running scripts, editing environment variables. ·
Basic Git - clone, commit, push, pull, branch. ·
Basic understanding of APIs - what a REST endpoint is, what JSON is, what an HTTP status code means. ·
Basic SQL - SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE, JOINs.

sources.content:
You still need logs and metrics, but you also need to see prompts, completions, token costs, latency per step, and tool-call traces because a bug might not be a stack trace, it might be a subtly wrong instruction fifteen tokens into a system prompt. ·
None of this makes classical software engineering obsolete. Quite the opposite production AI systems still need clean APIs, databases, authentication, caching, queues, and deployment pipelines. AI Engineering is best understood as software engineering plus a new, probabilistic component that needs its own discipline of prompt design, retrieval design, evaluation, and guardrails. This handbook treats it that way: roughly half classical backend engineering, half AI-specific engineering, glued together by production practices.
The Future of AI Engineering
A few trends are already visible and worth naming explicitly, because they shape how you should learn:
Agentic systems are becoming the default interface , not just chatbots. Instead of 'ask a question, get an answer,' production systems increasingly plan, call tools, retrieve data, verify their own output, and take multi-step actions with oversight. Understanding planning, reflection, and multi-agent coordination (Modules 17-20) is quickly becoming as fundamental as understanding REST APIs was a decade ago. 1.
Standardized interoperability layers are emerging. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is one of the clearest examples: instead of every framework inventing its own way to expose tools and data sources to a model, MCP standardizes it, the same way HTTP standardized how browsers and servers talk. Learning MCP now is analogous to learning REST in the early 2010s. 2.
Evaluation and observability are maturing into first-class disciplines , not afterthoughts. Companies that shipped AI features fast in 2023-2024 are now investing heavily in eval infrastructure because 'it seemed to work in the demo' doesn't survive contact with production traffic. 3.
Cost and latency engineering matter as much as accuracy. A model that's 2% more accurate but 5x more expensive and 3x slower is frequently the wrong choice. AI engineers increasingly need to reason about model routing, caching, and quantization/serving trade-offs, not just prompt quality. 4.
Security is catching up to a new threat surface. Prompt injection, data exfiltration through tool calls, and unsafe autonomous actions are real production risks, not academic curiosities.

sources.content:
This is the last 'pure backend' module before Module 3 introduces LLMs directly - treat it as the foundation everything from Module 5 onward is built on.
Why This Topic Matters
The gap between 'a script that works on my machine' and 'a service a team can maintain' is almost entirely software engineering discipline, not AI knowledge. Companies hiring AI Engineers consistently report that the differentiator between a junior and a senior candidate isn't who knows more about transformers - it's who can hand off clean, tested, documented code that someone else can safely modify six months later.
Industry Relevance
Production AI codebases fail in the same ways any production codebase fails: untested code that breaks silently, undocumented assumptions that create bugs, dependency chaos, and unreviewed changes that introduce regressions. The AI-specific parts (Modules 3+) sit on top of this foundation - if the foundation is weak, every module after this one inherits that weakness.
Common Misconceptions
'AI code is exempt from normal software engineering practices because it's experimental.' Prototyping can be loose; anything heading to production needs the same rigor as any other backend service. ·
'Testing LLM-integrated code isn't really possible since outputs vary.' You can't unit-test exact LLM output text, but you absolutely can and should test everything around it: input validation, retrieval logic, parsing, error handling, and use evaluation harnesses (Module 22) for the model-facing parts. ·
'Code review slows AI teams down too much given how fast things move.' The opposite is empirically true - teams that skip review on AI-integrated code accumulate prompt regressions and silent breakages far faster than teams that review, because the failure modes are less visible than a stack trace. ·
Learning Objectives
By the end of this module, you will be able to:
Structure a production-grade Python project using pyproject.toml and a src/ layout. 1.
Write effective unit, integration, and mocked-dependency tests with pytest . 2.
Use git effectively, including branching strategy, commit hygiene, and resolving conflicts. 3.
Apply SOLID-adjacent design principles pragmatically to AI application code. 4.
Set up linting, formatting, and pre-commit hooks ( ruff , black -equivalent, mypy ). 5.
Write clear technical documentation (README, docstrings, architecture decision records).

It is specifically designed to transition junior developers, data scientists, backend engineers, and AI enthusiasts into production AI and agentic AI engineers [cite_1]. The curriculum bridges classical backend engineering and modern probabilistic AI techniques [cite_2].
